c.tagline: Coastal capital of ceviche and colonial grandeur

taxi.fareNote: no meters; negotiate fare before boarding or use apps

emergency.note: Fire is 116; English-speaking operators are rare, so ask your hotel to call, and the Tourist Police (POLTUR) in Miraflores assist visitors.

hood_landmark.Miraflores: Huaca Pucllana adobe pyramid and the clifftop Malecón parks
hood_landmark.Barranco: Puente de los Suspiros (Bridge of Sighs) in the bohemian arts district
hood_landmark.San Isidro: El Olivar park's centuries-old olive grove
hood_landmark.Santiago de Surco: Parque de la Amistad with its landmark Friendship Arch
hood_landmark.San Borja: Museo de la Nación, Lima's monumental national museum

avoid.reason: Avoid La Victoria (Gamarra), Rímac and parts of Callao; downtown/Barrios Altos are risky after dark.
Pickpocketing in the centre and at bus terminals.

hood_desc: An upscale clifftop district over the Pacific that is the tourist heart, with parks, malls, restaurants, hotels and the Malecon boardwalk; suits first-time visitors wanting safety and walkability.
A bohemian coastal district that is Lima's arty corner, with colorful colonial houses, galleries, street art and nightlife; suits creatives, younger travelers and foodies.
Lima's polished financial and diplomatic district, leafy with the Olive Grove park, upscale hotels and business towers; suits business travelers and those wanting quiet luxury.
A large residential middle-to-upper-class district inland, home to malls and gated communities; suits longer-stay visitors and those visiting locals rather than tourist sights.
An orderly residential middle-class district with parks and the national museum, family-oriented and calm; suits travelers wanting an authentic base away from tourist crowds.
lodging: Casa Andina Premium Golf Los Incas

water.note: Avoid tap water; use sealed bottled water, including for brushing teeth.

transit.pay: Buy a reloadable card at station machines/counters (S/5 for Metro Line 1; a new unified interoperable card, S/7.50, became mandatory on Line 2 as of July 2026) - cash isn't accepted at turnstiles. Metro Line 1 rides cost S/1.50 (~$0.40); Metropolitano BRT fares run about S/2.50-3.50 (~$0.65-0.95).
transit.hours: Lines operate roughly 6am-11pm daily; there is no night service.

transit.m: Airport Express Lima coach to Miraflores, ~60 min

food.name: Ceviche
food.desc: Raw white fish cured in lime, chilli and leche de tigre with red onion, sweet potato and choclo. Order it at lunch, when the fish is freshest.

places.name: La Mar Cebicheria
places.note: Gaston Acurio's lunch-only cevicheria; the benchmark and no reservations, so arrive early.

places.name: Al Toke Pez
places.note: Nine-stool counter featured on Netflix's Street Food; huge value, queue down the street.

places.name: Pescados Capitales
places.note: Long-running favourite for classic ceviches and tiraditos in a relaxed garden setting.

food.name: Lomo saltado
food.desc: Beef stir-fried in a scorching wok with onion, tomato, soy and vinegar, served with fries and rice. Peru's great Chinese-Peruvian crossover.

places.name: Panchita
places.note: Acurio group criollo kitchen; polished versions of the classics plus a charcoal anticucho grill.

places.name: Isolina
places.note: Old-school taberna serving enormous sharing platters from handwritten family recipes.

places.name: Antigua Taberna Queirolo
places.note: Tavern from the 1880s; lomo saltado with a pisco sour here is a Lima rite of passage.

food.name: Anticuchos
food.desc: Beef heart marinated in aji panca and vinegar, skewered and grilled over coals, served with potato and choclo. Street food since colonial times.

places.name: Anticuchos de la Tia Grimanesa
places.note: Started as a Santa Cruz street cart, now a restaurant and the city's most famous name for anticuchos.

places.name: Tio Mario
places.note: Barranco institution grilling anticuchos and rachi; busiest in the evening.

places.name: Panchita
places.note: Charcoal grill turning out anticuchos and chicharrones in a comfortable sit-down setting.

food.name: Causa and criollo classics
food.desc: Chilled yellow potato pressed with lime and aji amarillo, layered with chicken or crab; alongside aji de gallina and carapulcra on the criollo table.

places.name: Isolina
places.note: Massive old-school portions of criollo cooking; go with a group and share everything.

places.name: El Bolivariano
places.note: Historic republican-era house, ideal for tasting a wide range of criollo dishes at once.

places.name: Panchita
places.note: Reliable, well-executed causa and aji de gallina for a first taste of the repertoire.

food.name: Chifa
food.desc: Peru's Chinese-Peruvian cooking: arroz chaufa, tallarin saltado and wantan. Best in the old Chinatown, where recipes go back generations.

places.name: Calle Capon
places.note: The original Chinatown street; Chinese-language menus and mostly local diners.

places.name: Wa Lok
places.note: Landmark chifa on Jiron Paruro, famous for dim sum and generous portions.

places.name: Chifa Titi
places.note: Long-established upmarket chifa favoured by Lima families for special occasions.

food.name: Pollo a la brasa
food.desc: Whole chicken marinated in soy, cumin and beer, roasted on a rotisserie and served with fries, salad and a battery of aji sauces.

places.name: Pardos Chicken
places.note: The best-known chain; consistent charcoal-roasted bird and famously good aji sauces.

places.name: La Panka
places.note: Slightly smarter take on the polleria formula with charcoal grill and craft beer.

places.name: Norky's
places.note: Everyday local polleria found across Lima; cheap, fast and open late.

food.name: Pisco sour
food.desc: Pisco shaken with lime, sugar syrup and egg white, finished with bitters. Invented in Lima in the 1920s and still the national drink.

places.name: Museo del Pisco
places.note: Bar and pisco school pouring flights and the classic Victor Morris recipe.

places.name: Antigua Taberna Queirolo
places.note: Tavern from the 1880s serving its own pisco; unfussy, cheap and thoroughly local.

places.name: Hotel Maury
places.note: One of the claimed birthplaces of the drink; a classic version in a faded grand bar.

food.name: Chicha morada
food.desc: Purple corn boiled with pineapple rind, cinnamon and clove, then chilled and sharpened with lime. Non-alcoholic and served with almost every meal.

places.name: Isolina
places.note: House-made chicha morada by the jug to go with the enormous criollo platters.

places.name: El Bolivariano
places.note: Traditional criollo house where chicha morada is poured as a matter of course.

places.name: Mercado de Surquillo
places.note: Market juice counters sell fresh chicha morada beside the fruit stalls for a few soles.

landmarks: Plaza Mayor de Lima
The historic main square with the Government Palace and Cathedral, heart of colonial Lima.
Lima Cathedral (Catedral de Lima)
A grand colonial-era cathedral facing the Plaza Mayor, one of the oldest in the Americas.
Basilica and Convent of San Francisco
Famous for its catacombs and stunning baroque facade in Lima's historic center.
Museo Larco (Larco Museum)
Renowned for its pre-Columbian art collection, set in an 18th-century mansion with beautiful gardens.
Huaca Pucllana
An ancient adobe pyramid complex in the middle of modern Miraflores, striking against the city skyline.
Parque del Amor (Love Park)
A clifftop park in Miraflores famous for the El Beso sculpture and ocean views, great at sunset.
Malecón de Miraflores
The scenic coastal boardwalk along the Costa Verde cliffs, popular for photos of the Pacific coastline.
Puente de los Suspiros (Bridge of Sighs)
A charming wooden footbridge in the bohemian Barranco district.
Circuito Mágico del Agua (Magic Water Circuit)
The world's largest fountain complex, spectacular at night with light and music shows.
Historic Centre of Lima
The UNESCO-listed colonial core with ornate wooden balconies and Spanish colonial architecture.

dom.op: Ferrocarril Central Andino (FCCA) - tourist Lima-Huancayo only

train.note: Peru has no national intercity passenger rail network. The only train from Lima is FCCA's occasional tourist service to Huancayo over the high Central Andes - it runs just a handful of departures a year, so check dates well ahead. For everyday intercity travel Peruvians use long-distance buses.

intl.to: Santiago (Chile), Buenos Aires (Argentina), Quito & Guayaquil (Ecuador), Bogotá (Colombia)

bus.note: Cruz del Sur is Peru's main long-distance operator and runs international coaches from its Javier Prado terminal in Lima; these are long hauls (Lima-Santiago is around two days) so carry your passport and check visa rules. Ormeño was historically the big international name but has become unreliable since its financial collapse - verify before booking.

ferry.note: There are no scheduled passenger ferry services from Lima; the port of Callao handles cargo and cruise ships only. Peru's passenger river boats operate in the Amazon (from Iquitos, Yurimaguas and Pucallpa), not from the Pacific coast.

half.name: Pachacamac
half.country: Lurín Valley, south of Lima, Peru
half.blurb: Sprawling pre-Inca temple complex and pyramids rising above the desert near the Pacific coast.

half.name: Palomino Islands
half.blurb: Wild rocky islets where thousands of sea lions gather and swimmers can join them.

full.name: Ballestas Islands
full.blurb: Rocky offshore islands teeming with sea lions, penguins and thousands of seabirds by boat.

full.name: Huacachina
full.blurb: Palm-fringed desert oasis surrounded by towering dunes perfect for sandboarding and buggy rides.

full.name: Caral
full.country: Supe Valley, north of Lima, Peru
full.blurb: Ancient pyramids of the Americas' oldest known civilization set in a quiet desert valley.
